chapter: Cab Calloway, Haiti and Sarah Vaughan
title: Issa El Saieh invites Budd to Haiti
summary: Issa El Saieh takes lessons from Budd and offers him a round trip, $200 a week and $100 for his wife to teach Haitian musicians.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Okay. So anyway, while I had received my 12 weeks notice, I had the fortune, the good fortune to meet a man named (Esa El-Sayee.) (ISSA EL SAIEH)

(Esa El-Sayee) was from Haiti, and he had come back to see Panama Francis because Panama Francis' father was a Haitian. And he came back to see Panama, and then so doing, I had the pleasure of meeting him. And he told me then, he says, Bud Johnson, he says, I sure like the way you play saxophone. He says, I play a little tenor saxophone myself. Can I take some lessons from you?

Well, I had entered into a studio with Eddie Bearfield and Jimmy Mundy and myself, we were in a studio on 48th Street between 6th and 7th Avenue in New York, and we called it BMJ, which is Bearfield, Mundy, Johnson, and we were going to try to set up an arranging and copying service and just write music for everybody. So he came up to the studio, and I used to do some teaching with him. So I mean I used to do some instructing for him, and when we got to know

each other a little better, he says, have you ever been to Haiti. I said, no, I have not. He says, well, you know, you should come down there. I said, well, gee, I would like to come down there. I said, but I can't just up and come down there. First place, I don't have the money. I'm married. And my roots are here in New York. I just can't jump up and leave. He said, well, would you like to come? I said, sure I would like to come. He says, you know, this is the only free Black republic in the world.

I said, yeah, I've read a little bit about Haiti, and I said, I would like to come down. He says, well, I'll tell you what I'll do. If you want to come down, I'll send you a round trip ticket and pay all your expenses and give you $200.00 a week. I said, what you want me to do for that? He said, well, I just want you to write a little bit and teach the Haitian musicians a little bit about a different kind of harmony and play in the band every once in a while. Well, he was -- this was 1947.

So I said, well, I'd like to go, I said, but, you know, my wife -- he says, well, I'll tell you. How much you think your wife need a week to live on while you're away? I said, well, she needs at least about $100.00 a week to run the house. He says, well, I'll give her $100.00 a week, and I'll pay you $200.00 a week and all expenses, and you come to Haiti. So sure enough, he says, well, I'm going home

tomorrow, and you'll hear from me in about three days. And sure enough, I heard from him in three days. He had sent me a Pan American ticket, round trip, and sent me the expenses, sent me a couple a hundred dollars for the expenses to come on down to Haiti.
Now to -- to -- to say what, tell you what he told me, I was the first jazz musician to go down to Haiti and instruct the musicians and play with them.
